evidence.quote: For much of its distance, SR 5 generally parallels the north bank of the James River, following the path of older colonial roads.

evidence.claim: plantation histories
evidence.quote: Some of the larger and older of the extant James River Plantations are along the route.

evidence.claim: Route 5 generally follows the James River’s north bank between Richmond and Williamsburg, along the paths of older colonial roads.
evidence.quote: For much of its distance, SR 5 generally parallels the north bank of the James River, following the path of older colonial roads.

evidence.claim: Outside those two cities, its entire length is a Virginia Byway.
evidence.quote: The entire length of SR 5 outside Richmond and Williamsburg is a Virginia Byway.

evidence.claim: The Virginia Capital Trail largely parallels it in a separate paved lane for walking and cycling, crossing streams and marshy ground on wooden bridges.
evidence.quote: The VCT largely parallels Virginia Route 5, a Virginia Scenic Byway, with its own physically separated, asphalt-paved lane

evidence.claim: The highway passes a sequence of historic James River plantations, including Berkeley, Westover and Sherwood Forest.
evidence.quote: From west to east, these are the Shirley Plantation, Edgewood Plantation, Berkeley Plantation, Westover Plantation, Evelynton Plantation, Belle Air Plantation, Piney Grove at Southall's Plantation, North Bend Plantation and Sherwood Forest Plantation.

evidence.claim: The state assembled this road in pieces, beginning in 1923 with a stretch west from Charles City toward Richmond numbered Route 41.
evidence.quote: The first piece of SR 5 was added to the state highway system in 1923, a portion of the road running west from Charles City for 18.5 miles (29.8 km) toward Richmond, and was numbered State Route 41.

evidence.claim: The Richmond–Williamsburg connection was complete in 1932 and became part of Route 5 in the 1933 renumbering.
evidence.quote: in 1932, the route was completed from Richmond to Williamsburg

evidence.claim: The Commonwealth Transportation Board designated Route 5 a Virginia Byway in 1975.
evidence.quote: 1975: The Commonwealth Transportation Board designates Route 5 as the Commonwealth's second Virginia Byway.

evidence.claim: The completed Capital Trail opened in October 2015, adding a dedicated route for cyclists and pedestrians.
evidence.quote: October 2015: Opening of the completed trail.

evidence.claim: Traveling east from Richmond, the corridor leads through Henrico into Charles City County, passing Shirley and then Berkeley and Westover.
evidence.quote: These are James City County, Charles City County, and Henrico County, moving from east to west

evidence.claim: At Charles City, Route 155 meets the byway beside the county’s courthouse-centered community.
evidence.quote: The community is centered on the Charles City County Court House

evidence.claim: Sherwood Forest lies farther east along the plantation sequence.
evidence.quote: North Bend Plantation and Sherwood Forest Plantation.

evidence.claim: Before Williamsburg, the Judith Stewart Dresser Bridge crosses the Chickahominy into James City County, a fixed span that succeeded the ferry and former drawbridge.
evidence.quote: Between Charles City County and James City County, it crosses the Chickahominy River via the Judith Stewart Dresser Bridge, a fixed-span bridge which replaced historic Barrett's Ferry and the former drawbridge.

evidence.claim: crossing streams and marshy ground on wooden bridges.
evidence.quote: includes about 30 wood bridges crossing streams and marshy areas.

evidence.claim: became part of Route 5 in the 1933 renumbering.
evidence.quote: In the 1933 renumbering, State Routes 41 and 835 both became part of a new State Route 5

evidence.claim: Route 155 meets the byway
evidence.quote: Charles City lies at the intersection of State Routes 5 and 155.

evidence.claim: At Berkeley’s old wharf, Harrison’s Landing, Oliver W. Norton and General Daniel Butterfield wrote the melody of Taps in 1862; Norton first played the bugle call there.
evidence.quote: In 1862 the Army bugle call "Taps" was first played, by bugler Oliver W. Norton; the melody was written at Harrison's Landing, the plantation's old wharf, by Norton and General Daniel Butterfield.

evidence.claim: Union troops occupied the plantation that year.
evidence.quote: During the American Civil War, Union troops occupied Berkeley Plantation

evidence.claim: The site’s earlier history includes the 110 people Benjamin Harrison V held in slavery when he died in 1791.
evidence.quote: Plantation owner Benjamin Harrison V held 110 people in slavery at the time of his death in 1791.

evidence.claim: The original quarters for enslaved people no longer survived when filmmakers built reconstructions for Harriet in 2018.
evidence.quote: Reconstructed slave quarters were built on the property in 2018 by the producers of Harriet, a movie about Harriet Tubman that was filmed in part at the plantation. The original quarters were no longer extant at that point.

evidence.claim: The mansion’s ground floor became a museum in the 1960s.
evidence.quote: The ground floor of the mansion was turned into a museum in the 1960s.

evidence.claim: Charles City’s courthouse remains at the center of the community where Routes 5 and 155 meet.
evidence.quote: The community is centered on the Charles City County Court House

evidence.claim: Earlier county courthouses stood along the James at Westover and City Point before the court moved to this inland community.
evidence.quote: courthouses were successively built along the James River at Westover, then City Point and in the 1750s in the town of Charles City.

evidence.claim: The old courthouse survives, but judicial use ended in 2007 and a new courthouse has been built.
evidence.quote: Used until 2007, it was one of only five courthouses in America that was in continuous use for judicial purposes since before the Revolutionary War. A new courthouse has since been built.

evidence.claim: Charles City remains the county seat and a center for services including the library and post office.
evidence.quote: Charles City serves as the central hub for local government in the county and as a central node for services including a library, bank, post office, and local schools.

evidence.claim: Here the Capital Trail briefly shares Courthouse Road near the government complex.
evidence.quote: In Charles City, the trail's pathway is shared by Courthouse Road for a short period near the Government Complex.

evidence.claim: where Routes 5 and 155 meet.
evidence.quote: Charles City lies at the intersection of State Routes 5 and 155.

evidence.claim: The old courthouse survives
evidence.quote: The original Charles City County Courthouse remains today.

evidence.claim: Charles City remains the county seat
evidence.quote: It is the county seat of Charles City County.

evidence.claim: John Tyler gave Sherwood Forest its name in 1842, saying it signified that the Whig party had outlawed him.
evidence.quote: John Tyler renamed the plantation Sherwood Forest in 1842. He said it signified that he had been "outlawed" by the Whig party.

evidence.claim: He retired here after leaving the White House in 1845.
evidence.quote: He retired there when he left the White House in 1845

evidence.claim: The plantation grew and processed tobacco using the labor of dozens of enslaved African Americans.
evidence.quote: The plantation complex was used by the Tylers to grow and process large amounts of tobacco. They owned dozens of African American slaves

evidence.claim: Recorded surnames of enslaved people include Armistead, Hall, Black and Short.
evidence.quote: The enslaved had the surnames Armistead, Hall, Black and Short.

evidence.claim: The house stretches 301 feet, including a long, narrow ballroom Tyler added for the Virginia reel.
evidence.quote: One of the house's claims to fame is its length; 301 feet (91 m).

evidence.claim: Restorers in the 1970s retained homemade storm windows after records identified them as Tyler’s work.
evidence.quote: Owners of the house who started restoring it in the mid-1970s started removing some home-made storm windows and then discovered from old records that Tyler had built them himself, so they kept them.

evidence.claim: including a long, narrow ballroom Tyler added for the Virginia reel.
evidence.quote: It is noted for its long, skinny ballroom, a "hyphen" Tyler had added to the house to accommodate the style of dancing popular then - what is today called "line dancing" but was then the "Virginia reel."

evidence.claim: John Jamieson bought Berkeley in 1907 after having served there as a drummer boy in McClellan’s army; his son later restored the house.
evidence.quote: John Jamieson, a lumber tycoon who as a youth had been at Berkeley as a drummer boy in McClellan's army, purchased the property in 1907.

evidence.claim: his son later restored the house.
evidence.quote: In 1925, his son Malcolm inherited the property, expending large sums of money to turn the ruined main house into a livable and stately home

evidence.claim: The community lies about two miles north of the James River, between Richmond and Williamsburg.
evidence.quote: 23 miles (37 km) west of Williamsburg, and about 2 miles (3 km) north of the James River.

evidence.claim: between Richmond and Williamsburg
evidence.quote: 30 miles (48 km) southeast of Richmond, 17 miles (27 km) east of Hopewell, 23 miles (37 km) west of Williamsburg

evidence.claim: Tyler bought the plantation from his cousin Collier Minge; the house has remained in the Tyler family since that 1842 purchase.
evidence.quote: John Tyler purchased the plantation in 1842 from his cousin Collier Minge

evidence.claim: the house has remained in the Tyler family since that 1842 purchase.
evidence.quote: The house has been in the Tyler family since it was purchased in 1842.

evidence.claim: Union troops occupied the plantation that year.
evidence.quote: During the American Civil War, Union troops occupied Berkeley Plantation, and President Abraham Lincoln twice visited there in the summer of 1862
